transcript:
This message comes from Odoo, the all-in-one business management software platform.
Whether you're a small or large business, Odoo gives you one flexible platform built to grow with you.
Try today for free at odoo.com/nprpodcasts.
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman.
We're learning more about the people who confronted a gunman during an elementary school shooting in Oregon on Thursday.
Police say their actions likely prevented further violence after three children and a teacher were killed.
Oregon Public Broadcasting's Bryce Doyle reports.
The gunman was a 16-year-old former student. Police say he jumped a fence with a shotgun and a backpack full of ammo.
He shot at a person in a pickup truck after the driver confronted him, then blasted his way through the school's locked doors.
The gunman then opened fire in a special education classroom.
Ben Police Chief Mike Krantz described what happened next.
A teacher in the classroom threw her cell phone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him.
She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed.
A parent who had seen the shooting outside the school followed the gunman inside and shot him multiple times with a handgun, killing him.
Two other people were shot, a 7-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher. They're receiving care at regional hospitals.
For NPR News, I'm Bryce Dole.
The latest White House press secretary is leaving the post just days after she began.
The White House says Katie Zachari is transitioning out of the position after questions emerged about her legal credentials.
Now, the White House will be without a press secretary, but as NPR's Emily Fang reports, that may not be a problem for President Trump.
He has shown he is very comfortable with the idea of mostly speaking for himself, regardless of whether that's good or bad for the Republican Party.
It's been almost two months, I should know, since Caroline Levitt, the last press secretary, left.
And so there have not been regular press briefings for months now.
And Trump frequently comes out and just directly takes questions from reporters at the White House, sometimes with very little notice.
That's NPR's Emily Fang with our report.
The Treasury Department has closed the books on the just-ended fiscal year.
As NPR's Scott Horsley reports, the government ran a deficit of almost $2 trillion.
The government spent a lot more money than it took in last year, $1.992 trillion more, to be exact.
That's the biggest annual deficit since the post-pandemic year of 2021.
Tax revenues were up 3 percent during the year, but spending grew twice as fast.
Just paying interest on the federal debt last year cost the government more than $1.3 trillion.
President Trump's double-digit tariffs did raise some money for the government,
but the Treasury had to refund almost half what those import taxes brought in
after the Supreme Court ruled many of the tariffs are illegal.
It's unusual for the government's finances to be this deep in the red when the country's not in a recession or fighting a widespread war.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
President Trump has signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy.
He told Congress Friday that the pause was in the national interest.
Trump personally signed a legislation just last month that sought to reduce the flow of finances, feeding the war against Ukraine.
You're listening to NPR News.
Brazil's government says rainforest loss in the Amazon has dropped 71 percent since 2023.
In a Friday announcement, they say satellite imagery also shows that 1,300 square miles of rainforest was lost in the year ending this past July.
That's the lowest annual loss since 1988.
Brazil's president made rainforest preservation a focus of his administration when he took office in 2023.
In the past few years, the FDA has approved several treatments that slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease.
But as NPR's Ping Huang reports, they're not reaching many people. They might help.
Antibody treatments help clear beta amyloid, a protein that builds up in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's.
They can slow the progression of dementia symptoms.
But researchers have found major disparities in who's getting them.
Dr. Brian Callahan is a professor of neurology at the University of Michigan.
Black patients and Hispanic patients are much less likely to have these medicines.
We're talking about 85 percent, 80 percent less likely.
Those are really big numbers.
The drugs are expensive, require intravenous infusion, and can cause serious side effects.
And Callahan says there's disagreement in the field about how much of a difference they really make.
But better drugs are coming, he says, so disparities should be addressed now.
The paper is published in the journal Neurology. Ping Huang, NPR News.
Game four of the American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and the Tampa Bay Rays has been postponed because of rain.
Game four will now be played Saturday at 8 p.m.
The Guardians have a 2-1 lead in the Best of Seven series after a 3-2 win on Thursday.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
